    Classical refinement 21

    G000001Zariski topologyTopology

    Classical refinement · Structure · Separated schemes of finite type over a separated Noetherian base S; see individual edge scope.

    Jointly surjective open immersions. On the finite-type site one can take finite families, including the empty cover of the empty scheme.

    Points. For the Gabber–Kelly finite-type site, the affine local test objects are spectra of local rings.

    References
    Stacks 020K · topologies on schemes · Gabber–Kelly, Definition 2.5, Theorem 2.6 and Table 1 · Stacks 020O · Zariski covering

    G000002Nisnevich topologyTopology

    Classical refinement · Structure · Separated schemes of finite type over a separated Noetherian base S; see individual edge scope.

    Completely decomposed étale families: every target point has a lift whose induced residue-field map is an isomorphism.

    Points. For the Gabber–Kelly finite-type site, the affine local test objects are spectra of henselian local rings.

    References
    Gabber–Kelly, Definition 2.5, Theorem 2.6 and Table 1

    G000004Smooth topologyTopology

    Classical refinement · Structure · Separated schemes of finite type over a separated Noetherian base S; see individual edge scope.

    Jointly surjective smooth families. Smooth surjections admit sections étale locally on the target, so their generated topology is already étale.

    Points. For the Gabber–Kelly finite-type site, the affine local test objects are spectra of strictly henselian local rings (by equality with étale).

    References
    Stacks 055U · étale-local sections of smooth morphisms · Stacks 020K · topologies on schemes · Stacks 021Z · smooth covering

    G000006Fppf topologyTopology

    Classical refinement · Structure · Separated schemes of finite type over a separated Noetherian base S; see individual edge scope.

    Jointly surjective flat morphisms locally of finite presentation. Over a locally Noetherian target, finite flat maps are finite locally free; in general use finite locally free maps in the generation theorem.

    G000007Fpqc topologyTopology

    Classical refinement · Structure · Separated schemes of finite type over a separated Noetherian base S; see individual edge scope.

    Flat families for which each affine open of the target is covered by images of finitely many quasi-compact opens in the sources that map into that affine open. In particular a faithfully flat quasi-compact morphism is a singleton cover.

    References
    Stacks 022A · fpqc coverings · Stacks 03NV · the fpqc topology · Stacks 022B · fpqc covering

    G000008Canonical topologyTopology

    Classical refinement · Structure · Separated schemes of finite type over a separated Noetherian base S; see individual edge scope.

    The finest topology for which every representable presheaf is a sheaf. A sieve covers precisely when it is universally effective epimorphic, tested by descent of maps into every object after each base change.

    References
    Stacks 00WO · representable sheaves and the canonical topology · Stacks 03NV · fpqc subcanonicity · Stacks 00ZA · canonical topology · Stacks 00Z9 · finest topology making given presheaves sheaves

    G000009Qfh topologyTopology

    Classical refinement · Structure · Separated schemes of finite type over a separated Noetherian base S; see individual edge scope.

    On the finite-type site one may take finite families of quasi-finite maps whose coproduct is a universal topological epimorphism (a quotient map after all base changes).

    Points. For the Gabber–Kelly finite-type site, the affine local test objects are spectra of absolutely integrally closed local domains.

    References
    Gabber–Kelly, Definition 2.5, Theorem 2.6 and Table 1

    G000012Prime-to-ℓ finite flat topologyTopology

    Classical refinement · Structure · Separated schemes of finite type over a separated Noetherian base S; see individual edge scope.

    Fix a prime ℓ. Use singleton finite flat surjections of constant rank d with ℓ ∤ d. Such maps are finite locally free in the finite-type Noetherian setting.

    References
    Gabber–Kelly, Definition 2.5, Theorem 2.6 and Table 1

    G000020ℓdh topologyTopology

    Classical refinement · Structure · Separated schemes of finite type over a separated Noetherian base S; see individual edge scope.

    Fix a prime ℓ. Adjoin prime-to-ℓ finite flat surjections to cdh covers.

    Points. For the Gabber–Kelly finite-type site, the affine local test objects are spectra of henselian valuation rings whose fraction fields have no nontrivial finite extension of degree prime to ℓ.

    References
    Gabber–Kelly, Definition 2.5, Theorem 2.6 and Table 1

    G000023Ph topologyTopology

    Valuative refinement · Structure · The common qcqs ambient category specified in the valuative diagram.

    Use Zariski covers and proper surjections as generators. The Stacks Project distinguishes ph from its finite-presentation h convention. Over the separated finite-type Noetherian site of the classical comparison these are the same generators used there for h.

    G000024Valuative (v) topologyTopology

    Valuative refinement · Structure · The common qcqs ambient category specified in the valuative diagram.

    For a map of qcqs schemes Y→XY\to X, test every Spec⁡V→X\operatorname{Spec}V\to X for a valuation ring VV. There must be an injective local map of valuation rings V↪WV\hookrightarrow W and a lift Spec⁡W→Y\operatorname{Spec}W\to Y over XX. For families, work affine locally on the target and take finite affine refinements whose disjoint union passes the test.

    References
    Bhatt–Mathew, The arc-topology · Stacks 0ETA · valuation lifting and comparison with fpqc and ph · Stacks 0EVM · affine inverse limits of h and ph covers

    Stacks index 0ETA 0EVM

    G000025Arc topologyTopology

    Valuative refinement · Structure · The common qcqs ambient category specified in the valuative diagram.

    Use the same lifting test but restrict both valuation rings VV and WW to rank at most one. Rank zero includes fields. For families use the corresponding affine-local finite refinement convention.

    References
    Bhatt–Mathew, The arc-topology

    G000026Qc Zariski basis siteSite

    Spectral spaces and locales · Structure

    For a qcqs scheme X, take its quasi-compact open subsets, with inclusions as arrows and finite open covers as covering families. Intersections stay in the basis, and restriction identifies Zariski sheaves with sheaves on this site.

    G000027Qc topology on locally quasi-compact spacesTopology

    Spectral spaces and locales · Structure

    Objects are locally quasi-compact Hausdorff spaces and maps are continuous. A family covers if every target point has a neighbourhood that is the union of images of finitely many quasi-compact subsets of the sources, in the sense that the union contains an open neighbourhood of the point.

    G000029Constructible topologyTopology

    Ramification data 3

    P000461Weak solution to eliminating ramificationProperty

    Ramification data · Predicate

    Fix an extension A⊂BA\subset B of DVRs with fraction fields K⊂LK\subset L and a finite extension K1/KK_1/K. Let A1A_1 be the integral closure of AA in K1K_1, and let B1B_1 be the integral closure of BB in (L⊗KK1)red(L\otimes_K K_1)_{\mathrm{red}}. For each maximal ideal 𝔮\mathfrak q of B1B_1 lying over a maximal ideal 𝔭\mathfrak p of A1A_1, the map (A1)𝔭→(B1)𝔮(A_1)_{\mathfrak p}\to(B_1)_{\mathfrak q} must be weakly unramified.

    T000029Fpqc topology is coarser than Valuative (v) topologyImplication

    Valuative topology refinement · The common qcqs ambient category specified in the valuative diagram.

    After base change to Spec⁡V\operatorname{Spec}V, a faithfully flat cover lifts the specialization from the generic point to the closed point. A valuation-ring extension dominating that lifted specialization gives the required square. For general families use an affine-local standard fpqc refinement.

    T000030Ph topology is coarser than Valuative (v) topologyImplication

    Given a proper surjection, choose a point over the generic point after base change to Spec⁡V\operatorname{Spec}V. Extend the valuation to the residue field of the chosen point and use the valuative criterion of properness. Zariski covers already satisfy the valuation test.

    T000031Valuative (v) topology is coarser than Arc topologyImplication

    Valuative topology refinement · The common qcqs ambient category specified in the valuative diagram.

    The valuation test can be expressed as lifting the specialization from the generic point to the closed point after base change to a valuation spectrum. Over a rank-one valuation ring, lifting that pair of points yields an extension of rank one. Thus an arbitrary-rank cover satisfies the rank-at-most-one test. See Proposition 2.1 and Corollary 2.5 of Bhatt–Mathew.

    Domain
    topologies on the category stated below
    Premise

    Conclusion
    Arc topology

    T000733Universal spectral submersion criterion for arc-coversEquivalence

    Valuative topology refinement

    Hypotheses. Let f:Y→Xf:Y\to X be a morphism of qcqs schemes.

    The map ff is an arc-cover if and only if for every map X′→XX'\to X from a qcqs scheme the base-changed map f′f' is surjective and any subset U⊆X′U\subseteq X' whose inverse image is quasi-compact Zariski open is Zariski open. The resulting open UU is quasi-compact because it is the continuous image of its quasi-compact inverse image.

    See also: Arc topology, Spectral space

    References
    Bhatt–Mathew, The arc-topology, Definition 2.14 and Proposition 2.19

    T000174Representability of the Grassmannian functorConstruction

    Schemes

    Hypotheses. Fix integers 0<k<n0<k<n. For each scheme SS, let G(k,n)(S)G(k,n)(S) be the set of isomorphism classes of locally free rank n−kn-k quotients of 𝒪S⊕n\mathcal O_S^{\oplus n}, with pullback on morphisms.

    Proof and context

    The quotient functor is a Zariski sheaf. For each choice of n−k coordinates, the locus on which their images are a basis is represented by affine k(n−k)-space. These open subfunctors cover the functor.

    T000520Exactness of module localizationConstruction

    Modules

    Hypotheses. Let RR be a ring, U⊆RU\subseteq R a multiplicative subset, and L→M→NL\to M\to N an exact sequence of RR-modules.

    The localized sequence U−1L→U−1M→U−1NU^{-1}L\to U^{-1}M\to U^{-1}N is exact.

    Proof and context

    An element sent to zero in a localization is killed by a denominator. Clearing such a denominator reduces exactness in the middle to exactness before localization.

    See also: Localization of a module, Flat module

    T000521Flatness under base changeCriterion

    Modules

    Hypotheses. Let R→R′R\to R' be any ring map and MM an RR-module. Let M′=R′⊗RMM'=R'\otimes_R M.

    If MM is flat over RR, then M′M' is flat over R′R'. If MM is faithfully flat over RR, then M′M' is faithfully flat over R′R'.

    Proof and context

    On R′R'-modules the functor M′⊗R′−M'\otimes_{R'}- identifies with M⊗R−M\otimes_R-. This transfers preservation of exactness and, in the faithful case, reflection of exactness.

    T000800Containment and lengths of latticesCriterion

    Modules

    Hypotheses. Let RR be a one-dimensional Noetherian local domain with fraction field KK, and let VV be finite-dimensional over KK. Let M⊆VM\subseteq V be a lattice.

    A submodule of VV containing MM is a lattice exactly when it is finitely generated, or equivalently when its quotient by MM has finite length. A submodule N⊆MN\subseteq M is a lattice exactly when M/NM/N has finite length. Two lattices have lattice intersection and sum. Lengths of quotients add along chains of nested lattices, and the distance between two lattices equals the difference of their quotient lengths by any common sublattice.

    T000535Classification of étale algebras over a fieldEquivalence

    Ring homomorphisms

    Hypotheses. Let kk be a field and SS a kk-algebra.

    k→Sk\to S is étale if and only if SS is a finite product of finite separable field extensions of kk. The empty product gives the zero algebra.

    Proof and context

    An étale algebra has finite-dimensional fibre over the unique point of the field, and its local factors are separable fields. Conversely, the product of finitely many such field extensions is étale.

    T000359Existence and uniqueness of algebraic closuresConstruction

    There exists an algebraic closure of FF. Any two are isomorphic over FF, generally by more than one isomorphism.

    T000365Independence of distinct multiplicative charactersCriterion

    Fields

    Hypotheses. Let FF be a field and GG a monoid. Let χ1,…,χn:G→(F,⋅)\chi_1,\dots,\chi_n:G\to(F,\cdot) be distinct monoid homomorphisms.

    These functions are linearly independent over FF. In particular, distinct embeddings of an extension into FF are FF-linearly independent as functions when their common domain and base are fixed.

    Proof and context

    In a nontrivial linear relation of minimal support, compare the relation at ghgh with the relation at hh multiplied by one of the character values at gg. Choose gg on which two characters in the support differ. Subtraction gives a nonzero relation with smaller support.

    See also: Field

    T000361Decomposition of an inseparable irreducible polynomialCriterion

    Polynomials over fields

    Hypotheses. Let PP be an inseparable irreducible polynomial over a field FF.

    The characteristic is p>0p>0. There is a maximal power q=prq=p^r with P(T)=Q(Tq)P(T)=Q(T^q), and QQ is irreducible and separable. The distinct roots of PP correspond to the distinct roots of QQ by the map x↦xqx\mapsto x^q in an algebraic closure.

    Proof and context

    If the derivative is zero, all exponents with nonzero coefficient are multiples of pp. Remove the largest common pp-power from those exponents. The resulting derivative is nonzero and irreducibility descends to QQ. Frobenius is bijective in the algebraic closure.

    See also: Irreducible polynomial, Separable irreducible polynomial, Separable degree of an irreducible polynomial

    Hypotheses. Let P∈F[T]P\in F[T] be nonconstant over a field FF.

    Field extensions

    Hypotheses. Let E/FE/F be a finitely generated field extension.

    Choose a finite transcendence basis SS of E/FE/F. Every finite subextension of the relative algebraic closure has degree over FF at most [E:F(S)][E:F(S)] by adjoining SS and using the tower law. The bounded degrees force the relative algebraic closure to be finite.

    Sites and presentations 64

    T000097The finite qc basis presents Zariski sheavesComparison

    Sites and presentations

    Every open is a union of affine opens. Finite intersections of quasi-compact opens are quasi-compact on a quasi-separated scheme, and every open covering of a basis object has a finite basis refinement. Restriction and the usual compatible-section extension therefore give inverse equivalences of sheaf categories.

    See also: Qcqs scheme, Qc Zariski basis site

    T000098Two uses of qc in site terminologyComparison

    Sites and presentations

    The finite open basis site uses inclusions of open subsets of a fixed scheme. The Stacks qc topology in Cohomology on Sites §21.31 uses continuous maps between locally quasi-compact Hausdorff spaces. Its comparison theorem uses the latter hypotheses, so it does not automatically apply to the Zariski space of a qcqs scheme.

    See also: Qc Zariski basis site, Qc topology on locally quasi-compact spaces

    T000100The profinite site and condensed setsComparison

    Sites and presentations

    Finite jointly surjective families are closed under pullback and composition, and include the empty family covering the empty space. With a fixed strong limit size bound, the sheaf condition on this site gives the corresponding condensed sets. This compares sites of spaces and is not a refinement relation on schemes.

    T000102Giraud’s characterizationComparison

    Sites and presentations

    A Grothendieck topos is characterized, in a fixed universe, by the Giraud axioms: a small generating family, universal small colimits, disjoint coproducts and effective equivalence relations (with the usual categorical hypotheses). A site gives a presentation, not a unique presentation.

    T000104Hochster representationEquivalence

    Sites and presentations

    Hypotheses. Work in classical set theory. Consider a topological space XX and commutative rings with identity, allowing the zero ring.

    XX is spectral if and only if it is homeomorphic to Spec⁡(A)\operatorname{Spec}(A) for some commutative ring AA. The equivalence concerns existence of a realization as a topological space.

    Proof and context

    Every spectral space is homeomorphic to the prime spectrum of a commutative ring, and every prime spectrum is spectral. The assertion concerns the underlying topological space, without specifying a canonical ring or recovering a scheme structure.

    See also: Spectral space, Affine, Coherent locale, Prime spectrum of a ring

    References

    T000105Coherent locale and spectral space dualityEquivalence

    Sites and presentations

    Hypotheses. Use classical prime ideal separation, spectral spaces with spectral maps, and coherent locales with maps whose inverse image preserves compact opens.

    Taking the locale of opens and taking the space of points are inverse equivalences. The compact elements of the frame are the quasi-compact opens of the spectral space.

    Proof and context

    Classically, bounded distributive lattices are dual to spectral spaces with spectral maps. Prime ideals give the points, and the lattice is recovered as the quasi-compact opens. Ideal completion gives the corresponding coherent frame; the spatial interpretation uses classical prime ideal separation.

    See also: Locale, Coherent locale, Spectral map, Spectral space

    T000109Little and big Zariski comparisonSite comparison

    Sites and presentations

    Hypotheses. Let SS be a scheme. Choose a big Zariski site as in Blechschmidt §15, containing the opens of SS, and let Sh⁡(S)\operatorname{Sh}(S) denote the little Zariski topos.

    The geometric morphism π:Zar⁡(S)→Sh⁡(S)\pi:\operatorname{Zar}(S)\to\operatorname{Sh}(S) is connected and local. The direct image π∗\pi_* is restriction and has a fully faithful right adjoint, giving a section of π\pi.

    Proof and context

    For the big site chosen in the thesis, §16 constructs the comparison with the little topos and describes how the structure sheaves and internal statements transform. The restricted affine finite presentation model has its own specified hypotheses and is not being identified here with the entire category of schemes over an arbitrary base.

    See also: Petit Zariski site, Affine finite presentation Zariski site, Gros Zariski site

    T000148From covering families to covering sievesSite comparison

    Sites and presentations

    Hypotheses. Let 𝒞\mathcal C be a site specified by covering families satisfying the isomorphism, composition and base-change axioms.

    A sieve is covering precisely when it contains the sieve generated by some covering family. The resulting Grothendieck topology has the same sheaves as the covering-family presentation.

    Proof and context

    The axioms on the families give the maximal-sieve, pullback and local-character axioms. A matching family on a cover extends to its generated sieve by compatibility on the pullbacks. Uniqueness and existence on a larger covering sieve can then be tested on a contained covering family and its pullbacks.

    T000152Comparison lemma for sitesEquivalence

    Sites and presentations

    Hypotheses. Let u:𝒞→𝒟u:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D be continuous and cocontinuous. Require that two arrows with the same image under uu agree after a cover of their common source, and that an arrow u(U′)→u(U)u(U')\to u(U) locally lifts after a cover of U′U' in 𝒞\mathcal C. Require every object of 𝒟\mathcal D to have a cover by objects in the image of uu.

    The morphism Sh⁡(𝒞)→Sh⁡(𝒟)\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal C)\to\operatorname{Sh}(\mathcal D) obtained from the cocontinuous functor uu is an equivalence.

    Local lifting and equality of arrows identify the sheafified morphism data on image objects. The covering condition then reconstructs each sheaf on the target from those local data by descent.

    T000155Geometric stalks on small and big étale sitesConstruction

    Sites and presentations

    Hypotheses. Let SS be a scheme, with the big site formed in a fixed size convention.

    The geometric points of SS give a conservative family for the small étale site. On the big étale site use the geometric points of all objects T→ST\to S, evaluating the stalk after restriction to TeˊtT_{\text{ét}}. Exactness of sequences of abelian sheaves on the small site is equivalent to exactness at the geometric stalks.

    Proof and context

    A stalk is the filtered colimit over pointed étale neighbourhoods. A germ that lifts or vanishes does so after shrinking such a neighbourhood.     T000353Algebraicity in towersCriterion

    Field towers

    Hypotheses. Let F⊆E⊆LF\subseteq E\subseteq L be field extensions and let a∈La\in L.

    If aa is algebraic over FF then it is algebraic over EE. If L/FL/F is algebraic then L/EL/E is algebraic. If both L/EL/E and E/FE/F are algebraic then L/FL/F is algebraic.

    T000362Algebraic separability in towersCriterion

    Field towers

    Hypotheses. Let F⊆E⊆LF\subseteq E\subseteq L be a tower of algebraic field extensions.

    Elements separable over FF are separable over EE, and separability of L/FL/F gives separability of both E/FE/F and L/EL/E. If L/EL/E and E/FE/F are separable, then L/FL/F is separable.

    Changing the base upward replaces a minimal polynomial by a divisor. For transitivity, pass to finite intermediate extensions containing the elements and coefficients in question, then use the embedding count.

    X000034The rational numbers as an integer moduleExample

    Modules

    𝐐\mathbf Q is a localization of 𝐙\mathbf Z, so it is flat and torsion free. Finitely many rational generators have bounded denominators. Every map 𝐐→𝐙\mathbf Q\to\mathbf Z vanishes by divisibility. A nonzero projective module is a summand of a free module and therefore has a nonzero coordinate map to 𝐙\mathbf Z. At every maximal ideal the residue fibre of 𝐐\mathbf Q vanishes.

    Has: Module over a Noetherian ring, Module over a domain, Flat module, Torsion-free module over a domain

    X000060A reduced zero-dimensional scheme with a non-Hausdorff Zariski spaceExample

    Schemes

    Put R=∏n≥1𝐅2R=\prod_{n\geq 1}\mathbf F_2. This Boolean ring has only maximal primes. Let ene_n be the idempotent supported on coordinate nn, and let U=⋃n≥1D(en)U=\bigcup_{n\geq1}D(e_n). The opens D(en)D(e_n) are disjoint nonempty singletons, so UU is not quasi-compact. Glue two copies of Spec⁡(R)\operatorname{Spec}(R) along UU by the identity. The two affine charts make the glued scheme quasi-compact, reduced and of dimension zero. Their intersection is UU, so the scheme fails quasi-separatedness. The criterion of Stacks 0CKV then excludes Hausdorffness.

    Has: Krull dimension at most zero, Quasi-compact, Reduced
    Fails: Quasi-separated, Hausdorff underlying space, Spectral, Profinite underlying space

    X000011A two-point spectral space that is not profiniteExample

    Topological spaces

    The spectrum of a discrete valuation ring has one generic point and one closed point. It is spectral, but the generic point is not closed. In the patch topology both singletons are open, so that topology is finite discrete.

    Has: Spectral space
    Fails: T₁ space, Hausdorff space, Profinite space

    X000012A compact Hausdorff space that is not profiniteExample

    Topological spaces

    The real interval [0,1] is compact and Hausdorff, but connected and has more than one point. It cannot be profinite, since the finite discrete coordinate quotients of a profinite space separate its points.

    Has: Quasi-compact space, Hausdorff space
    Fails: Totally disconnected space, Profinite space, Spectral space

    X000014The p-adic integers are profinite but not extremally disconnectedExample

    Topological spaces

    The p-adic integers are the inverse limit of the finite discrete quotient rings modulo powers of p. The subset of nonzero elements with even p-adic valuation is open. Its closure adds 0, which is not interior because every neighbourhood of 0 also contains elements of odd valuation.

    Has: Profinite space
    Fails: Extremally disconnected space

    Sources and method

    The catalogue records hypotheses and primary references. Browse all 21,446 registered tags in the Stacks Project index, with bidirectional source references and definition clauses. Source references are editorially distinct from implications.

    Codes are local to this atlas and independent of display order. P identifies a predicate; G a structure or construction; T a theorem; X an example. Pi-Base links show their own external IDs and indicate whether the definition is the same, applies to the underlying space, or only gives a comparison. Search Pi-Base P000050 to match that external ID specifically.

    Within each refinement diagram, “A is coarser than B” means every A-covering sieve is B-covering in the stated category. The checker compiles conjunctions to Horn clauses, indexes occurrences by signed fact, and records a proof step for each inference. It can use an explicit negative hypothesis or test the opposite of the goal by refutation. Incompatible premises are reported as such. A counterexample requires a cited object satisfying all hypotheses and failing the conclusion. An unresolved result is unknown in the recorded theory.

    Comparisons across categories and results whose hypotheses have no machine-readable encoding are presented as references. The inference is relative to the verified rules in the catalogue; it is not a decision procedure for algebraic geometry.

    Predicate entries separate the object domain, hypotheses and conclusion. One Stacks definition can give rise to several distinct predicates. Conjunctions and stated equivalences join predicates without merging their IDs. The explicit logical presentation takes inspiration from Blechschmidt’s account of internal languages; the implication checker is classical and uses only the explicitly stated scope.

    Design references: Grassmannian.info’s classification and item-level bibliography · Pi-Base record format · Pi-Base prover · Dowling–Gallier, Horn clauses.

    Cohomology reading guides: Holmström’s crystalline index and étale index; see also Berthelot, Cohomologie cristalline and Milne, Lectures on Étale Cohomology.
